lesson.title: How far to trust a reading

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the swarm tighten round where the meter centres instead of round the true value when you make each bead the mean of four readings on a meter that reads high.
interactive.title: Offset and repeats
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on simulated readings drawn as beads. Each bead is one simulated reading of a battery bank's float voltage. Say its charger holds it at 27.00 V. That true value is drawn as a dashed line. A rule on screen makes each reading. It starts from the true value and adds any offset the meter has. It then adds the random error times the sum of twelve small nudges. Each nudge lies between minus a half and plus a half. The total is read to the meter's step of 0.01 V. Here the random error is 0.04 V. That is the standard deviation of one reading's scatter. Fifty readings pour from the hopper through the peg field. They land on the beam and rise into a swarm. Each bead takes its colour from where it lands against the mean. Beads below the mean take one colour, and beads above take another. The nearer a bead sits to the mean, the fainter its colour. A key says so. A reading past 27.10 V goes to a small pile named over, past a gap at the end of the scale. One lands there when the meter reads 0.03 V high. The beam balances on its fulcrum at the mean. A choice, Each bead is the mean of 1, 2 or 4 readings, averages that many readings into each bead. As the number rises, the pegs close in. A slider, Meter reads high by, runs from 0 to 0.03 V in steps of 0.01 V. It moves the hopper, so every reading lands that much high. A button, Drop a fresh batch, on screens 1, 3 and 9, draws fifty new readings from the same rule, with a soft tick for each. A window behind the hopper is as wide as an example meter's accuracy, ±(0.1% of the reading + 2 digits). 0.1% of 27.00 V is 0.027 V. Two digits of 0.01 V are 0.02 V. So the window reaches 0.047 V either side. An ink bracket over the swarm is the result. It is the mean of the fifty beads, plus or minus 2 × the beads' standard deviation ÷ √50. A wide bracket under the beam marks where most beads fall: the mean ± 2 standard deviations. The drawing gives the mean's value in bold. Two tiles give the result's ± and the beads' standard deviation. The first is labelled Result ±. Each tile has its rule as a hint. The screens. 1, show: fifty readings pour and rise into a swarm round 27.00 V. Most land within about 0.08 V either side. A single reading could be any one of these beads. 2, a puzzle: a single reading off this meter says 27.06 V. What can you say about the true voltage? Offered: it is probably within about 0.08 V of 27.06 V; it is 27.06 V; and the charger is set 0.06 V high. Hint when wrong: every bead came from 27.00 V, yet many landed well away from it. 3, show: make each bead the mean of 2, then 4 readings. Their random errors point different ways and partly cancel. The swarm narrows to about seven tenths of its width, then to half. It still centres on 27.00 V. The spread of a mean is the spread of one reading divided by the square root of how many are averaged. Its finished picture shows each bead as the mean of four. 4, a puzzle: one reading's random error is 0.04 V. Each bead is the mean of four readings. What is the beads' standard deviation? Offered: 0.02 V; 0.01 V, dividing by four; and 0.04 V, unchanged. Hint: divide by the square root of how many readings each bead averages. 5, show: back to one reading a bead. The result bracket appears over the swarm. The result is the mean of all fifty, so by the square-root rule it spreads 0.04 ÷ √50. Twice a spread either side catches about 95%. So the bracket reaches 2 × 0.04 ÷ √50 either side of the mean. With √50 about 7.07, that is about 0.011 V. The value is given to the same decimal place as its ±: 27.001 ± 0.011 V. The wide bracket under the beam shows where most single readings land, about 0.08 V either side. 6, a puzzle: the fifty readings give a result of 27.001 ± 0.011 V. The next single reading says 27.05 V. Is something wrong? Offered: no, single readings scatter much wider than the result; yes, it lies outside the result so it is faulty; and yes, the meter has started reading high. Hint: the result brackets the mean of fifty, not each reading. Single readings land within about 0.08 V. 7, show: a choice, The meter reads to 0.01 V or 0.05 V. On the 0.05 V meter the beads hop into bricks one step wide. The step named under the beam is the meter's resolution. Rounding alone can put a reading up to half a step, 0.025 V, from what the meter sensed. The mean of many still lands close to 27.00 V. A fine step is not the same as an accurate meter. Its finished picture shows the bricks. 8, a puzzle. Its lead says what accuracy is: how far the meter may be out. It is written as a percentage of the reading plus a few digits. Each digit is one display step. A rating of ±(2% + 2) on a reading of 100.0 V allows 97.8 V to 102.2 V. The puzzle: a meter rated ±(1% + 3 digits) shows 50.0 V, reading to 0.1 V. Where could the true voltage be? Offered: 49.2 V to 50.8 V; 49.5 V to 50.5 V; and 49.9 V to 50.1 V. Hint: take 1% of 50.0 V. Then add three steps of the last digit, 0.1 V each. 9, show: the accuracy window appears behind the hopper. At 27.00 V it reaches 0.027 + 0.02 = 0.047 V either side. A meter within its rating can centre anywhere inside it. Set the meter to read 0.02 V high. The hopper slides inside the window, and the whole swarm shifts across. Make each bead the mean of four, and the swarm tightens round 27.02 V. That is where the meter centres. The result, 27.020 ± 0.006 V, misses the dashed true value. Each fresh batch misses it too. Its finished picture shows the meter reading 0.02 V high, with each bead the mean of four. 10, a puzzle: this meter reads 0.03 V high. You make each bead the mean of four readings instead of one. Where does the result centre now? Offered: near 27.03 V, with a narrower bracket; near 27.00 V, as averaging cancels the error; and near 27.015 V, halfway. Hint: the offset lands on every reading the same way, so it lands on their mean too. 11, show: with four readings a bead, a dashed example upper limit appears at 27.02 V. Slide the offset. At 0 and 0.01 V the whole result bracket sits below the limit. The opening batch is picked for that. At 0.02 V the bracket overlaps the limit. From the readings alone, the true value could be either side, so it shows neither a pass nor a fail. At 0.03 V the bracket sits above, and the readings say fail. Yet the true value stays 27.00 V, under the limit. The hidden offset alone pushed the result over. So a real bracket must also take in the meter's accuracy. Its finished picture shows the meter reading 0.02 V high and the bracket overlapping the limit. 12, a mixed puzzle: a result is 0.82 ± 0.03 Ω at 95%. The example maximum is 0.84 Ω. What does it show? Offered: neither a pass nor a fail, as the bracket reaches past 0.84 Ω; a pass, as 0.82 Ω is under 0.84 Ω; and a fail, as part of the bracket is over. Hint: compare the whole bracket, 0.79 to 0.85 Ω, with the limit. 13, a mixed puzzle: your meter reads to 0.05 V and reads 0.02 V high. You switch to one that reads to 0.01 V with the same 0.02 V offset. What gets better? Offered: each reading shows a finer step, but the offset stays; the mean of many readings moves closer to the true value; and both, finer steps and no offset. Hint: a finer display shows smaller steps, but it does not move where the meter centres. Some screens show an idea, and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. On a 360 px phone the answers, the two tiles and the three bead choices wrap onto more lines, so no word ever splits.
interactive.ignores: The readings are simulated from the rule on screen, not taken from a real battery. The 27.00 V, the meter's accuracy and the limit are examples. The offset here is set by hand and drawn. A real meter's offset is hidden until you check it against a known reference. It can change with the range, the temperature and the size of the reading. A real battery's voltage would wander a little too. Here it holds still. Twelve nudges make an even scatter with no long tails. The doubled bracket suits fifty readings. For a handful of readings, the factor of 2 is raised a little. A full uncertainty also combines the meter's accuracy and every other influence into one figure. That uncertainty budget is not shown here.

explain.text:
No single reading can tell you the true value. A reading can carry two kinds of error. They behave differently when you repeat. Random error throws each reading a different way, so averaging repeats shrinks it. A steady offset throws every reading the same way, so averaging leaves it exactly where it was. Say a charger holds a battery bank at 27.00 V. Each reading has a random error of 0.04 V, measured as its standard deviation. Most single readings land within about 0.08 V of the true value. Now make each reading the mean of four. Their random errors point different ways, so they partly cancel. They are random, so they rarely cancel fully. The spread of a mean of n readings is the spread of one reading divided by √n.[^3] That holds when each reading's random error is independent of the others. Four readings halve it, to 0.02 V. Two readings cut it only to about 0.028 V. So to halve the spread again you need four times as many readings, not twice as many.

The same rule says how well the mean of fifty readings is pinned down. Divide the 0.04 V spread by √50, which is about 7.07. Then double it. That gives about 0.011 V. This doubled bracket is the usual one: the mean ± 2 × the standard deviation ÷ √n. It catches where the meter centres about 95% of the time. A stated [[uncertainty]] needs two parts: a width and how confident you are. One example is 20 cm ± 1 cm at 95%. So fifty readings give a result of 27.000 ± 0.011 V. The value is given to the same decimal place as its ±. That bracket is far narrower than the 0.08 V either side where most single readings land. The result says how well the mean is known. The scatter says how far one reading wanders.

Now say the meter reads 0.02 V high. The same influence lands on every reading, so the whole swarm shifts across. That is a [[systematic error]]. Repeating teaches you nothing extra about it. Make each bead the mean of four, and the swarm tightens round 27.02 V. That is where the meter centres. The result is now 27.020 ± 0.006 V. It misses the true 27.00 V. Yet a meter 0.02 V high can still be within its accuracy. Accuracy is the most its maker allows it to be out. A digital meter usually states it as a percentage of the reading plus a few digits. Each digit is one step of the display. An accuracy of ±(2% + 2) on a reading of 100.0 V allows anything from 97.8 V to 102.2 V.[^2] That display step is the meter's [[resolution]]. It is the finest change the meter can show. A finer step shows more detail, but it does not move where the meter centres. A check against a known reference finds the offset.

This matters most against a limit. The bracket from repeats covers only the random part. A full uncertainty also takes in the meter's accuracy and every other influence. If that whole bracket sits on one side of the limit, the reading shows which side the value is on. If it overlaps the limit, the true value could be on either side. Then the reading shows neither a pass nor a fail. Working out a full uncertainty is called an uncertainty budget. This simplified picture leaves it out.

**Averaging repeat readings shrinks random scatter by the square root of how many you take. No number of repeats removes a steady offset. So a result's uncertainty must also take in the meter's accuracy, at a stated confidence.**

analogy.text: Think of measuring a cable run with a tape whose hook is bent back 2 mm. Each time you read it, your eye lands a little differently, so the readings scatter. Measure ten times and average. The eye's wobble mostly cancels. Every reading is still 2 mm too long, so the average is 2 mm too long as well. No amount of averaging fixes that. A look at the hook does.
analogy.breaks: A bent hook adds the same length to every measurement. A meter's offset can grow with the size of the reading. That is why accuracy has a percentage part. It can also shift with the range or the temperature. And you can see a bent hook. A meter's offset stays hidden until you check it.

practice.text:
- Work safely, as your procedure sets out. Take several readings the same way: same leads, same points, same range.
- Find their mean and standard deviation.
- Divide the standard deviation by the square root of how many readings you took. Then double it. That is the random part of the result's bracket, at about 95%.
- Work out the meter's accuracy at that reading. Take the percentage of the reading, then add the digits times one step of the display.
- Repeats cannot shrink the accuracy. Check the meter against a known reference to find any offset.
- Set the whole bracket against the limit. If it overlaps the limit, the reading alone shows neither a pass nor a fail. If the random part is the larger, take more readings. If the accuracy part is, use a more accurate meter.

**Rule of thumb:** four times the readings halves the random bracket. No number of readings removes an offset.

**Worked example:** take ten readings of a battery bank's float voltage. The example meter is rated ±(0.1% + 2 digits) and reads to 0.01 V. Their mean is 27.04 V and their standard deviation 0.03 V. The random part is 2 × 0.03 ÷ √10. With √10 about 3.16, that is about 0.02 V. For the accuracy, 0.1% of 27.04 V is 0.027 V. Two digits add 0.02 V, so the accuracy is 0.047 V. Adding both straight gives a cautious bracket for the true voltage. It runs from about 26.97 V to about 27.11 V. A full budget combines them more tightly. The example maximum is 27.15 V. The whole bracket is below it, so it shows a pass. With fewer than about 30 readings, the factor of 2 is raised a little. Here that would not change the answer.

**Common mistakes**
- Quoting one reading as the value, with no bracket.
- Expecting more readings to cancel a meter that reads high.
- Taking the last digit for the accuracy. The display step is the resolution. Accuracy is usually wider.
- Dividing by the number of readings instead of its square root.
- Reading the result's bracket as where single readings land.
- Calling a clear pass when the bracket touches the limit.
- Calling a small rise between two single readings a real change. First set it against each reading's bracket.

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the swarm tighten round where the meter centres instead of round the true value when you make each bead the mean of four readings on a meter that reads high.

checks.label: The spread of a mean is the spread of one reading divided by the square root of the number of times the measurement was repeated: over 2,000 beads from the rule on screen, single readings spread 0.04 V, and means of 2 and of 4 readings spread 1 ÷ √2 and 1 ÷ 2 as widely, within 5%

Systematic: the same influence affects the result for each of the repeated measurements, so you learn nothing extra just by repeating. With the meter 0.01, 0.02 or 0.03 V high, every reading of the batch lands exactly that much higher, and so does the mean, whether each bead is the mean of 1, 2 or 4 readings; the scatter is unchanged

An accuracy of ±(2% + 2) means a reading of 100.0 V can be from 97.8 V to 102.2 V; by the same rule ±(1% + 3 digits) on 50.0 V read to 0.1 V gives 49.2 V to 50.8 V, as the rating puzzle draws it, and the example meter's ±(0.1% + 2 digits) at 27.00 V read to 0.01 V reaches 0.047 V either side, the width of the window behind the hopper

Worked by hand from this batch: one reading a bead gives a mean of 27.00 V, an SD close to 0.04 V and a result of ± 0.011 V (2 × 0.04 ÷ √50, with √50 about 7.07), with 49 of the 50 within 0.08 V of 27.00 V and one at 27.06 V; two a bead about seven tenths as wide; four a bead half as wide and ± 0.006 V; 0.02 V high and four a bead, 27.02 ± 0.006 V, missing 27.00 V; against 27.02 V the result sits below, below, across and above as the offset rises; on the 0.05 V meter every reading is a whole step and the mean moves under 0.002 V; 0.82 ± 0.03 Ω runs 0.79 to 0.85 Ω, across 0.84 Ω

Drawn true: settled, the fulcrum sits under the mean and the beam is level at every setting; the hopper over 27.00 V plus the offset, inside the window; the limit line at 27.02 V; the mean's value clear of every bead and no dashed line through a label; a reading past the scale sits in its overflow pile; over 60 batches at every setting no two beads touch, none is under r 3.2 and each stays in its room; the deepest colours reach 3:1 and the palest still shows; each puzzle accepts only its right answer and gives nothing away before it; every motion settles within 5 s

applied.problem: Overstated absolutes: random errors 'never' cancel fully (a mean of four can land exactly on 27.00 V); a reading 'easily' lands 0.08 V out (2 SD, about 1 in 20); the 1/√n rule needs independent errors; accuracy is not always %+digits; 'the meter is still within its accuracy' asserts an unstated spe…

Worked example says the true voltage 'could be anywhere' in a 95%-plus straight-sum bracket; the standard method combines in quadrature, so this is a cautious bracket. More readings cannot help when the accuracy part dominates, as here. Pass/fail rules vary by job; no safety line on a live battery.
Screen 7 says accuracy is written as a percentage of the reading plus digits as if always so; the source says accuracy 'may' include digits, and some meters state it otherwise.

notes.problem: 'Confidence of a doubled bracket, 95%' cites source 1, whose quote gives a 95% example but does not say that ±2 standard errors gives 95%; it is textbook-certain only for many readings (about 95.4% for a normal pile).
'Readings below which textbooks raise the factor, about 30' is a textbook rule of thumb (the t-distribution), kept as assumed; no research source states it.
